differences.title: 1. UPDATE MECHANISM
differences.leftDesc: React re-renders components when state/props change, driven by Hook updates and concurrent scheduling. It builds a new virtual tree, then commits minimal DOM changes based on diffing during the render/commit phases.
differences.rightDesc: Vue tracks reactive dependencies at the property-access level using Proxies. When a reactive value changes, it marks only dependent effects as dirty, then batches a targeted re-render for consumers.

differences.title: 2. GRANULARITY
differences.leftDesc: React’s default update granularity is component-level: a state change triggers re-render of the owning function component, potentially cascading through parents unless memoization prevents it. Diffing remains structural.
differences.rightDesc: Vue’s reactivity is more granular because dependencies are recorded per accessed reactive key. Computed/effects re-run only where relevant, often reducing unnecessary component-wide work for localized state changes.

differences.title: 3. STATE MUTATION SEMANTICS
differences.leftDesc: React encourages immutable updates so referential equality changes can be detected by reducers, memo, and state comparisons. Mutating existing objects can lead to missed updates or stale memoized derivations.
differences.rightDesc: Vue allows direct mutation of reactive objects/arrays. Proxies intercept reads/writes, so changing a field automatically notifies dependents without requiring you to replace whole objects for reactivity.

differences.title: 4. BATCHING & FLUSH
differences.leftDesc: React batches state updates during event handlers (and more broadly in concurrent mode), coalescing multiple Hook updates into fewer renders. The scheduler decides when to flush, yielding back to the browser when needed.
differences.rightDesc: Vue batches reactive-triggered updates using a job queue and flush timing (typically next microtask). Multiple mutations within a tick coalesce, and rendering occurs when the queue flushes.

differences.title: 5. DERIVED STATE
differences.leftDesc: React often uses useMemo/useCallback to cache derived values, but dependencies must be declared correctly. Incorrect dependency arrays can cause recomputation or stale values; derived state typically lives in render logic.
differences.rightDesc: Vue computed creates a cached, reactive derivation that re-evaluates lazily when its dependencies change. It tracks what it reads during evaluation, preventing needless recomputation and stale derivations.

differences.title: 6. RENDER TARGET
differences.leftDesc: React renders to a virtual tree and relies on reconciliation to determine what changed. Even with optimizations, it must reconcile element-by-element using keys and component boundaries to update the real DOM.
differences.rightDesc: Vue templates compile into render functions with DOM patching strategies. Reactivity drives which parts of the render output re-run, and Vue’s patching updates only affected DOM segments within the component’s scope.

differences.title: 7. COMPATIBILITY WITH CONCURRENT WORK
differences.leftDesc: React’s concurrent features (e.g., React 18) can interrupt, resume, or defer rendering work. This impacts how state transitions schedule renders and how UI remains responsive under heavy updates.
differences.rightDesc: Vue’s async rendering model integrates with its job queue: updates are scheduled and flushed in controlled batches. It’s designed to keep the UI consistent while efficiently processing reactive invalidations.
